item.title: The independence still waiting to be completed
item.description:
On the morning of July 31, in a hotel in Dhaka, the United States Special Envoy for South and Central Asia met India's high commissioner to Bangladesh. The conversation lasted about 90 minutes and took place the day before the envoy called on Bangladesh's prime minister, and that evening the Indian envoy flew to Delhi for consultations. Neither side described what was discussed.
Nothing improper occurred. Diplomats meet, and it is the business of every state to advance its own interests. India was pursuing India's. Washington was pursuing America's. Beijing continues to pursue its own across the region. States behave like states, and there is nothing in that to resent.
What stayed with me was simpler, and quieter.
A consequential conversation about this region took place on Bangladeshi soil, and Bangladesh was not part of it -- and few in Dhaka seemed to think this worth remarking upon.
Consider, too, the arrangement itself. The American envoy holds two appointments simultaneously: Ambassador to India, and Special Envoy for South and Central Asia. Delhi recognizes the first and has been visibly uneasy about the second; when he announced in June that he looked forward to working closely with India's incoming envoy in Dhaka, a former Indian foreign secretary objected publicly, observing that American ambassadors to India do not customarily approach Indian envoys posted to third countries.
The doctrine has been clear for our country, as recently stated by our foreign minister: Bangladesh would never strengthen ties with one country at another's expense, and seeks good relations with all while advancing its own interests. It is the right doctrine, and I believe it is sincerely held. The question is whether we have built anything capable of carrying it.
There is reason for doubt, and it does not require any accusation to see.
In February, Bangladesh signed a trade agreement with the United States that lowered our tariff to 19% -- a real and welcome gain for an economy under strain. But the agreement also carried conditions that made it harder for Dhaka to move closer to certain other countries, China foremost among them.
Four months later, in Beijing, China proposed the Bangladesh-China-Myanmar Economic Corridor: Road and rail from Yunnan through Myanmar to Chittagong and Mongla. Our foreign minister said, correctly and carefully, that Bangladesh was examining the proposal and had taken no position.
Read those two facts together. In February we accepted relief on the condition that our future alignments be constrained. In June we were offered something that tests exactly that constraint. And in July, envoys of two other powers sat in a Dhaka hotel and discussed the region for 90 minutes without us.
This is what the loss of strategic autonomy actually looks like. Not occupation. Not humiliation. A sequence of individually reasonable decisions, each defensible on its own terms, which together narrow the range of choices available to the country later.
Why do we keep arriving here? I do not believe it is chiefly the fault of foreign capitals, and I do not think it is a failing of the present government alone. It is older than that.
Across five decades, our politics has repeatedly sought abroad the confidence it could not settle at home. Where authority rests on a mandate that is contested rather than trusted, where institutions are staffed by loyalty rather than merit, where the press must weigh its words, a government's standing does not rest securely on the consent of its own citizens. It has to be supplemented. And the supplement is always foreign -- Delhi in one decade, Washington in another, Beijing in a third. It is paid for in policy.
That is the mechanism, and it explains why strategic autonomy is not, in the first place, a question of foreign policy at all.
A government confident of its standing at home does not need to be reassured of its standing abroad, and cannot be moved by the withdrawal of that reassurance. We have rarely sustained such confidence for long. Until we do, our negotiating position will keep being set somewhere other than Dhaka.
Nor can a country negotiate freely if it cannot discuss its own affairs freely. The most telling feature of that week was the quiet around it -- the ordinary questions a confident nation asks aloud, unasked.
Into that silence rushed rumour: Within a day, versions of events were circulating that the record does not support. When careful reporting recedes, the public appetite to know does not. It merely goes unfed.
I have lived in Sweden long enough to be careful about what I claim for it. Swedish foreign policy is not unconstrained. In 2024 Sweden abandoned two centuries of non-alignment and joined NATO -- not in tranquillity, but because Russia had made the older position untenable. Geography pressed on Stockholm as it presses on Dhaka, and Stockholm yielded to it.
The difference is not that Sweden escaped constraints. It is that the decision was argued in the Riksdag (parliament), reported by a press nobody had to be brave to read, and afterwards owned by Swedes as their own. No foreign envoy settled it in a hotel room, and no citizen was left to guess what had been agreed on his behalf.
That is the whole of what I am asking. Not the freedom to do as we wish -- no country has that. The capacity to make a constrained choice in our own name, in the open, and to answer for it afterwards. That does not require Sweden's wealth. It requires institutions we could build at our present income.
Two proposals, then. They are modest, and they can be refused.
I write from Stockholm, and I should be honest about what that distance means. I am a Swedish citizen. I will very likely never see Bangladesh again. But my mother is there, and I was born there, and a man does not choose which soil made him.
Watching that week gave me no pride. I have looked for a gentler way to say it and not found one. I do not ask that Bangladesh be admired. I ask that Bangladesh not be bullied -- by anyone.
We won our political independence in 1971 at a cost this generation cannot fully imagine. But independence was never the achievement of a single morning. It is renewed, or quietly given away, in the ordinary decisions of ordinary years -- in what we sign, in what we ask, in what we permit to be discussed about us in rooms we are not invited into.
Bangladesh's future will not be settled in Washington, Delhi, or Beijing. It will be settled in Dhaka, or it will not be settled at all.
That is the independence still waiting to be completed.
Rajani K Saha writes from Sweden and is a practising physician.

item.title: Deeds not words
item.description:
Experts at a climate and nature conservation event recently stating Bangladesh to move beyond speeches and into real, measurable action could not be more accurate.
While the statements were made with regard to climate action, this is a lesson that Bangladesh ought to learn across all sectors, and in the way our nation operates. Whether the issue is climate resilience, pollution control, river restoration, or urban management, we have spent years producing policies, committees, and declarations with little to no implementation.
We have never suffered from a shortage of plans. We continue to suffer from a shortage of delivery.
The consequences of this gap are visible everywhere. Ambitious commitments followed by limited follow‑through continue to damage our nation, and it is time we recognized this insidious pattern and started changing how we operate.
We simply cannot afford this cycle any longer. Climate impacts are intensifying, environmental degradation is accelerating, and the cost of inaction is rising.
We need execution, not more rhetoric. We need projects staying within time and budget, enforcing regulations consistently, and holding institutions accountable for results rather than announcements.
Equally important is coordination, as too many initiatives fail because agencies work in silos, duplicating efforts or leaving critical gaps. We need a culture where agencies realize that they are not working to generate social media posts about inaugurations but actually to help the people and the country.
Bangladesh also needs stronger monitoring and transparency. Public reporting on project progress would build trust and ensure accountability. Citizens should not have to rely on sporadic updates or vague assurances.
The message from experts is clear: Bangladesh must shift from promises to performance. We possess the knowledge and the policies. What we need now is discipline, coordination, and sustained political will.

item.title: Fixing our energy future
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s latest remarks -- stressing the efficient use of existing resources and a decisive shift toward energy diversity -- comes at a critical time for our nation, and must be heeded.
To say that Bangladesh is navigating an increasingly difficult energy landscape would be an understatement, with recent gas shortages across the nation only the latest example. To that end, the message from the PM should be clear: Our country must diversify, modernize, and use what it already has with far greater discipline.
While the Matarbari power plant, which is where the PM delivered his remarks, is not without its share of criticism - which are legitimate given the eventual need to shift away from fossil fuel-generated energy sources - what is also true is that for addressing our immediate energy needs, its efficient operation is critical.
Bangladesh must embrace true energy diversity, and for the short run, that does, unfortunately, include fossil fuels as well. However, the transition to renewable sources must be more than rhetoric; the present BNP government has ambitious goals regarding renewable energy, but we will not be close to those goals without action.
The PM’s emphasis on using existing resources efficiently also points to a long‑standing problem: Poor maintenance, system losses, and mismanagement. Before adding new megaprojects, which had become the norm, Bangladesh must fix the basics -- reduce transmission losses, upgrade aging lines, and ensure that every kilowatt generated is actually delivered.
Energy is not just a sector but the backbone of economic stability. Without reliable power, industries falter, investment slows, and public frustration grows.
The responsibility now lies with policy-makers and institutions to act with urgency, discipline, and foresight. Bangladesh must move beyond short‑term fixes and commit to a diversified, efficient, and resilient energy future.

item.title: The anatomy of anarchy
item.description:
When a water bottle flew through the stage lights at Manik Mia Avenue and struck Hasan, the legendary frontman of Ark, directly in the face, the collective gasp across social media felt like a moment of sudden shock.
Images of the veteran rock icon -- a man whose voice carried generations through heartbreaks and youth rebellions -- wiping away the splashed water while continuing his set with dignity made the rounds online. People reacted with outrage, calling it an unprecedented disgrace.
Was it really unprecedented?
If we look past our collective amnesia, the bitter truth emerges: We did not suddenly lose our concert etiquette yesterday. We were always like this.
Cast your mind back to the late 1990s and early 2000s, the supposed golden era of Bangladeshi band music.
Memory has a way of painting those years in warm, nostalgic tones, but the reality on the ground was far uglier. I remember a time when audiences routinely pelted performers with tomatoes, rotten eggs, and footwear if a set list didn't match their immediate whims.
I remember when the infamous " genjams " -- violent, uncontrolled brawls -- were an expected, almost routine feature of every major show.
I remember the Russian Cultural Centre (RCC), once a sacred sanctuary for underground rock, having to shut its doors and ban live music after audiences smashed wooden chairs, chain-smoked indoors, and defaced the venue.
I remember the casual, normalized hooliganism in the pit: The aggressive dhakka mere shamne jaowa (shoving past people to get to the front), or the predatory culture of meyeder shathe jor kore gaaye ghesha -- unwanted physical proximity and harassment that made live music an unsafe space for women.
I remember the toxic rivalries where sabotaging or "eating up" another band’s stage slot ( slot khawa ) was celebrated as a victory.
I remember crowds weaponizing the chorus of "bhua, bhua" simply for the cheap thrill of humiliating a musician who poured their soul into a mic.
And I remember the vile, derogatory catcalls tossed without second thought at female artists brave enough to step under the spotlight.
Those dark tendencies never disappeared; they merely mutated. For a large demographic, the core concept of a concert has never been about artistic appreciation or community harmony.
It has been an excuse for anarchy, power trips, and unchecked bad behaviour.
This toxic entitlement is not unique to Bangladesh, nor is it a localized phenomenon.
Across South Asia and the Western world, stage violence and disrespect toward performers reveal a global strain of spectator hostility.
In India, classical legends and modern pop stars alike have faced rowdy crowds breaking barricades and hurling objects when expectations weren't met.
In the West, the phenomenon has reached epidemic levels in recent years.
We saw Bebe Rexha needing stitches after being struck in the eye by a cellphone thrown from the crowd; Harry Styles hit in the face by flying objects on stage; Florence Welch routinely dodging debris; and country artist Kacey Musgraves facing audiences who treat the stage as a target range.
What drives a person to hurl a heavy plastic bottle at an artist mid-song? It is rarely about the music itself.
At its core, this behaviour stems from a perverse mix of entitlement, malice, and a deep-seated desire to exert power over someone vulnerable on a pedestal.
An artist on stage is in a fundamentally defenseless position: Blinded by spotlights, wearing headphones or ear monitors, and focused on delivering a performance.
For an unruly element in the crowd, throwing something or creating chaos is the ultimate act of cheap thrill-seeking.
It turns the performer from a subject of admiration into a target of objectification -- a human canvas for an audience member's unearned dominance.
In our context, this behaviour is further fueled by a historical lack of accountability.
When venue managers, security guards, and event organizers normalize crowd violence as "just fan energy," they enable a culture where artists are viewed as public property rather than human beings deserving of basic safety.
Yet, as disheartening as the sight of Hasan bhai being targeted was, the aftermath offers a glimmer of genuine hope.
In the late 90s, an incident like this would have been buried in local gossip or brushed off as just another messy night at a concert.
Today, the landscape is radically different.
Thanks to the power of social media and pervasive smartphone documentation, these acts of violence can no longer hide in the shadows of a dark venue.
Within hours, the clip went viral. But more importantly, the public response was swift and uncompromising.
The overwhelming sentiment across the nation was not amusement, but collective shame and fierce condemnation.
Major musicians, the Bangladesh Musical Bands Association (Bamba), and thousands of ordinary concertgoers spoke out in unison, demanding accountability, better security infrastructure, and criminal identification of the perpetrator.
People are finally calling out the toxicity that we ignored for decades. We are refusing to let the bad behaviour of a few ruin the cultural spaces of the many.
Changing a deeply ingrained mindset will not happen overnight; unlearning decades of normalized disrespect will take time and intentional effort.
But identifying the disease is the first step toward curing it.
Hasan bhai responded to the assault with the grace and humility of a true legend, urging forgiveness and refusing to let hate stop the music.
His grace should not serve as a free pass; rather, it should serve as our mirror.
Let the outrage over his dignity be the definitive tipping point.
Let it mark the death of our culture of anarchy, and the birth of an era where respect for the artist on stage is non-negotiable.
Wafiur Rahman looks after the business desk at Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: When seeing is no longer believing
item.description:
A recent social media post by a Bangladeshi judge offers a revealing glimpse into the growing role of artificial intelligence (AI) in legal practice.
Reflecting on his courtroom experience, the judge recounted that a lawyer had submitted a Naraji petition drafted with the assistance of AI.
He observed that it was perhaps the first petition he had encountered in several months that presented coherent and well-reasoned legal arguments.
When asked whether AI had been used, the lawyer responded with an embarrassed smile.
The growing acceptance of AI
The judge further noted that the increasing workload faced by lawyers often leaves them with limited time, forcing legal assistants to prepare petitions such as applications for Naraji , discharge, and bail in haste, often at the expense of quality.
The judge went on to describe AI as a “second brain” for legal professionals. While seemingly modest, this observation captures a profound shift taking place within the legal profession.
It reflects not only the growing acceptance of AI as a practical tool for legal research and drafting but also signals the technology’s expanding influence on the administration of justice.
More importantly, it foreshadows a future in which artificial intelligence may become an integral part of legal decision-making, raising important questions about the opportunities and the risks it presents for courts and the justice system.
That observation captures a broader reality. AI is no longer a futuristic technology confined to research laboratories. It has become part of everyday governance, legal practice, and public administration.
Bangladesh has already begun integrating AI into public services. AI-assisted e-traffic prosecution system ,which automatically detects traffic violations through smart cameras, is one notable example. Such initiatives promise greater efficiency, transparency, and consistency in law enforcement.
Yet technological progress also raises difficult legal questions. As AI becomes increasingly capable of generating, analyzing, and manipulating digital content, the justice system must confront an uncomfortable reality. How should courts determine what is real when technology can convincingly manufacture what appears to be truth?
This question is no longer hypothetical. Courts will inevitably encounter AI-generated audio recordings, videos, photographs, and documents.
Judges, investigators, prosecutors, and defence lawyers will increasingly be required to distinguish authentic evidence from sophisticated digital fabrications.
Establishing authenticity
The challenge is no longer simply about admitting digital evidence. It is about establishing its authenticity.
Bangladesh’s Evidence Act, 1872 , amended in 2022, recognizes electronic records as admissible evidence. The amendment represented an important step towards modernizing evidentiary law.
However, it was enacted before generative AI, deepfakes, voice cloning, and large language models became mainstream technologies.
Consequently, while the Act recognizes digital records, it offers no specific legal framework for AI-generated evidence, algorithmic decision-making, or synthetic media. The result is a significant evidentiary gap.
The recently enacted Cyber Security Act, 2026 has not filled this gap either. Although the legislation addresses a range of cyber-related offences, it provides no legal definition of artificial intelligence and contains no comprehensive framework governing AI-generated evidence or the evidentiary risks posed by synthetic content.
These concerns are reinforced by the research of Dr Salwa Haque, who argues that AI should assist, not replace, human decision-making power.
AI systems learn from historical data, and where that data reflects bias, inequality, or inaccuracy, those shortcomings may be reproduced by the algorithm itself.
For that reason, AI cannot replace human judgment in evaluating credibility, weighing evidence, or appreciating the broader social and factual context of a dispute.
Perhaps the most immediate challenge comes from deepfakes and voice cloning.
Today, sophisticated AI systems can create remarkably convincing videos depicting individuals accepting bribes or produce audio recordings that faithfully imitate the voices of judges, politicians, and business leaders.
None of these events may have occurred in reality. More troubling still, current detection technologies cannot reliably identify every advanced deepfake.
Consequently, the traditional assumption that seeing is believing has become increasingly unreliable.
For centuries, courts have relied upon the principle of chain of custody to safeguard the integrity of evidence. Judges examine not only the content of evidence but also where it originated, how it was stored, and whether it remained unchanged before reaching the courtroom.
AI fundamentally complicates this process. If an entire video is artificially generated rather than merely edited, conventional forensic analysis may fail to reveal the deception.
This exposes another weakness in the existing legal framework. Section 65B of the Evidence Act requires certification of computer-generated records to establish their authenticity.
That requirement remains important, but in the age of artificial intelligence it is no longer sufficient.
Courts may also need to know which AI model generated the content, what training data it relied upon, whether the output can be independently reproduced, and whether the system has undergone independent auditing. Existing evidentiary rules do not require these safeguards.
Another significant concern is the so-called “ black box problem.” Many advanced AI systems cannot explain how they reach particular conclusions. From the perspective of procedural fairness, this creates a profound dilemma.
A defendant has the constitutional right to examine and challenge the evidence presented against them. Yet meaningful cross-examination becomes difficult if neither the court nor the technology’s developer can explain how an algorithm reached its conclusion.
Equally important is the problem of algorithmic bias. AI is often perceived as objective because it relies on data rather than emotion.
In reality, AI inherits the strengths and weaknesses of the data on which it is trained. International research has repeatedly demonstrated that biased datasets can produce discriminatory outcomes, particularly in facial recognition technologies and predictive decision-making systems.
If similar technologies are adopted in Bangladesh, an obvious question arises, who bears legal responsibility when an innocent person is wrongly identified by an algorithm?
Legal reform alone will not solve these challenges. Institutional preparedness is equally critical. Bangladesh’s forensic institutions, including the criminal investigation department (CID) and the police bureau of investigation (PBI) have made significant progress in digital forensic investigations over the past decade.
However, AI-generated manipulation demands a different level of expertise. Advanced AI detection systems, machine-learning forensic techniques, metadata analysis, and independent expert evaluation will become indispensable components of future criminal investigations.
International developments offer useful guidance
Canada, despite being one of the world’s leading AI research hubs, has not yet enacted a comprehensive national AI statute. Instead, Canadian courts rely on existing privacy, human rights, consumer protection, and administrative law to resolve AI-related disputes.
The European Union has adopted a different strategy through the AI Act, introducing a risk-based regulatory framework that imposes strict obligations regarding transparency, accountability, and human oversight for high-risk AI systems.
Both approaches demonstrate an important lesson, the goal is not to prohibit artificial intelligence but to regulate it in a manner consistent with democratic values and the rule of law.
Bangladesh is currently developing a national AI policy, an encouraging development. Nevertheless, meaningful reform requires more than policy declarations.
The Evidence Act should recognize AI-generated evidence as a distinct evidentiary category. Section 65B should be modernized to require disclosures concerning AI models, training data, software versions, audit trails, and independent forensic verification where appropriate.
Simultaneously, investment in forensic laboratories and specialised training for judges, prosecutors, investigators, and lawyers should become a national priority.
The Constitution of Bangladesh guarantees equality before the law, due process, personal liberty, and the right to a fair trial. These guarantees must remain fully effective regardless of technological change.
No person should be convicted solely on the basis of an opaque algorithmic assessment that cannot be independently scrutinized or challenged.
Every major technological revolution has compelled the law to evolve. Artificial intelligence represents perhaps the most transformative challenge yet because it changes not only how information is communicated but also how evidence is created, interpreted, and evaluated.
Bangladesh should embrace artificial intelligence, but it must do so with caution. The real challenge is ensuring that technological innovation strengthens, rather than weakens, the pursuit of justice.
In the age of artificial intelligence, courts are no longer tasked only with separating truth from falsehood. Increasingly, they must distinguish reality from highly convincing digital illusion.
Technology can become one of the justice system’s most powerful allies, but it can never replace judicial independence, human reasoning, or the rule of law.
Those principles, not algorithms, must remain the ultimate guardians of justice.
Kazi Latifur Reza is Head, Department of Law, Bangladesh University.

item.title: Swapon: US a key partner in Bangladesh’s economic progress
item.description:
Information and Broadcasting Minister Zahir Uddin Swapon on Monday said the United States is one of Bangladesh’s closest and most important partners in the country’s current economic progress.
“The partnership between the two countries plays a highly important role in economic prosperity, garment exports, expatriate remittances and foreign direct investment (FDI),” he told a views-exchange meeting with interfaith leaders at Gournadi Catholic Church in Barisal.
US Ambassador to Bangladesh Brent T. Christensen addressed the event as the guest of honor.
Swapon said the United States is the largest single export destination for Bangladesh export-oriented garment industry.
At the same time, Bangladeshi immigrants living in the United States regularly send substantial amounts of remittances, strengthening the country’s economy, he added.
In addition, a significant share of the total foreign direct investment (FDI) coming to Bangladesh originates from the United States, making a major contribution to the country’s overall economic process, he said.
The minister welcomed and congratulated Christensen on his visit to Gournadi Upazila in Barisal, the minister’s home area. Government officials, heads of religious institutions and local political leaders were present at the event.

item.title: IDLC, Friendship sign MoU to establish solar village in Gaibandha
item.description:
IDLC Finance PLC and Friendship NGO have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to establish a solar village in Mollar Char, Gaibandha, Rangpur.
The project aims to provide clean energy, solar-powered irrigation facilities and community infrastructure in the remote, climate-vulnerable char area.
The MoU was signed by M Jamal Uddin, CEO and Managing Director of IDLC Finance PLC, and Runa Khan, Founder and Executive Director of Friendship, at IDLC Finance's corporate head office in Gulshan, Dhaka.
The initiative will be implemented during 2026-2027 as part of IDLC's Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) commitment under its Environment and Climate Change Mitigation and Adaptation pillar.
The project includes a 30 kWp solar-powered micro-grid system, 2 solar irrigation pumps, prepaid energy meters for 70 households, 1 electric husking machine, 2 electric threshers and refrigeration support for local shops and pharmacies.
It will also include capacity-building initiatives for 10 local para-solar technicians to support community-based operation and maintenance.
Through Friendship Farmer Clubs and Sustainable Economic Development Hubs, para-solar technicians will receive training, while additional electricity will create opportunities for climate-smart agriculture.
The initiative is expected to directly benefit approximately 315 people, including farmers who will receive solar-powered irrigation across 10 acres of land, households receiving electricity and community members using shared electric farming machinery.
“The lack of reliable electricity and modern irrigation infrastructure at Mollar Char has been significantly constraining agricultural productivity by increasing production costs. It is also limiting economic opportunities. I hope our partnered efforts with Friendship for the Solar Village project will make a difference to the community and uplift their lives in the long term,” said M Jamal Uddin, CEO and Managing Director of IDLC Finance PLC.
Runa Khan, Founder and Executive Director of Friendship, said: “On the chars, resilience is built through practical solutions that give people greater control over their own lives. Friendship's micro-grid with solar irrigation pumps brings this reality to fruition. Reducing farming costs by 1/3, bringing safety to the community and reliable energy into homes. Uplifting livelihoods and turning clean technology into opportunity, dignity and greater economic security.”
Most households in the char primarily depend on agriculture and cultivate leased land. Although some households have basic home solar power, it is mostly incapable of powering all household appliances simultaneously.
As the community remains beyond the reach of the national electricity grid, landless farmers have to rely on diesel-powered irrigation, resulting in higher seasonal and transportation costs and operational inefficiencies.
The integrated model aims to provide households with renewable energy while supporting sustainable livelihoods.
The project builds on Friendship's experience in renewable energy interventions, including the development of Bangladesh's first solar micro-grid and the operation of 7 solar villages across Kurigram and Gaibandha.
The Mollar Char solar village project is another addition to this work. Through the partnership, IDLC Finance and Friendship aim to expand renewable energy access for vulnerable communities while addressing energy access, agricultural productivity, livelihoods and climate resilience in remote char communities.

item.title: Pori Moni drug case: Charge hearing deferred to Sept 29
item.description:
A Dhaka court has set September 29 for the hearing on charge framing against film actress Pori Moni and two others in a drug case filed with Banani Police Station.
The hearing was scheduled for Monday at the court of Judge Md Robiul Alam of Dhaka Special Judge Court-10. However, Pori Moni’s lawyer Nilanjana Rifat (Surabhi) sought an adjournment.
In her petition, the lawyer said Pori Moni could not appear in court as her child had developed a fever after receiving a vaccination. She also cited her child’s birthday as another reason for her absence.
The court granted the time petition and fixed September 29 for the next hearing, the lawyer said. In 2021, Pori Moni made headlines after accusing a businessman of attempting to rape her. Days later, on August 4 that year, the Rapid Action Battalion (RAB) raided her residence and said it had recovered alcohol and drugs. She was subsequently arrested and charged in a drug case. She was released after spending about a month in jail.
On October 4 that year, CID Inspector Kazi Golam Mostafa, the investigation officer in the case submitted a charge sheet against Pori Moni and two others.
On January 5, 2022, the court framed charges against the three accused and ordered the trial to begin. The other two accused are Pori Moni’s manager Ashraful Islam Dipu and her maternal uncle Kabir Hossain Howlader. RAB-1 official Majibor Rahman, the complainant in the case, has already begun testifying before the court.
After the charges were framed, Pori Moni filed a petition with the High Court seeking the cancellation of the case. On March 1, 2022, the High Court issued a rule and stayed proceedings against her for three months.
The higher court later ordered that the charges be framed afresh in the case.

item.title: Days of heavy rain leave at least 16 dead in Philippines
item.description:
Floods, landslides and accidents driven by a nine-day downpour equivalent to more than a month’s worth of rain in some areas have killed at least 16 people in the northern Philippines, rescuers said Monday.
The rains, exacerbated by tropical storms, have led to school and government office closures across the main island of Luzon and flooding in the streets of the capital Manila.
Seven of the deaths occurred in the resort of Baguio, as a rain-drenched mountainside collapsed on three houses, city rescuer Esther Banawe told AFP. Three people remain unaccounted for.
“Rescue efforts are continuing, but they are doing it manually because of the heavy rain,” she said, adding that work was being supervised by a designated safety officer for fear of further landslides.
State weather forecaster Dan Villamil said rains in the vacation town, four hours north of the capital, were already 47% higher than normal for the whole month.
“The rainfall recorded for August 1-9 was highest in Baguio, with an accumulated 1,413.2 millimeters (56 inches),” he said, adding the city’s typical downpour for the month was 963.2 millimeters.
Parts of Metro Manila had recorded rain equivalent to about 90% of a typical August, he added.
Landslides killed six other people elsewhere on Luzon, while another drowned, one was hit by a falling tree, and one was electrocuted, according to a civil defense office tally.
While heavy rain continued to fall Monday evening, Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon told a news conference that floodwaters were receding.
“Our interventions are continuing, but we really need to fix the years and decades’ worth of faulty flood mitigation interventions,” Dizon told reporters, referencing a scandal over bogus flood-control projects that have cost taxpayers billions of dollars.
The Philippines is the first major landmass facing the Pacific cyclone belt, and the archipelago is hit by an average of 20 storms and typhoons each year, putting millions of people in disaster-prone areas in a state of constant poverty.
Scientists say human-driven climate change is making extreme weather more frequent, prolonged and intense.

item.title: Indian students step up exam protests in Jharkhand
item.description:
Indian students marched towards the state assembly in Jharkhand on Monday, escalating protests over alleged irregularities in government recruitment examinations, with several students also on hunger strike.
Protests in Ranchi, capital of the eastern state home to more than 33 million people, began on July 29, days after a youth-led “cockroach” movement in New Delhi forced the resignation of the national education minister.
At least six protesters are on hunger strike, including student leader Devendra Nath Mahto, 33, who has been fasting for more than a week.
“We want the whole system to change,” Mahto said, as quoted by Indian media, demanding an end to the use of a private company that conducts tests for state civil service.
On Monday, hundreds of police guarded the assembly behind barbed-wire barricades, after repeated talks between the protesters and the state government failed to reach an agreement.
Large crowds of students chanting slogans marched towards the state assembly.
The protesters are demanding the cancellation of several examinations conducted by a private company on behalf of the state government, as well as an investigation by federal police into their conduct.
Jharkhand Chief Minister Hemant Soren has sought to defuse the protests by accepting some demands, while several members of the civil service body overseeing the examinations have stepped down.
“Every problem can be resolved through dialogue,” Soren said in a speech on Sunday.
The New Delhi protesters, organized by the online Cockroach Janta Party, rallied for 36 days over alleged failures in India’s examination system, before the then education minister Dharmendra Pradhan stepped down -- giving the movement an unusual victory and turning examination integrity into a major political issue.
The Jharkhand protests echo those demands, reflecting wider frustration among young Indians who see government examinations as a key route to employment in a country where millions compete for limited public-sector jobs.
The New Delhi protests challenged Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party, but the Jharkhand rallies are demanding change from the state government, which stands in opposition to the BJP.

item.title: Ukraine drone strike on Russian oil-refining city kills 13
item.description:
A Ukrainian drone strike on the central Russian region of Tatarstan killed at least 13 people in one of the deadliest attacks carried out by Kyiv since the war began more than four years ago.
Kyiv said it had struck an oil refinery in the industrial city of Nizhnekamsk, more than 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) away from the Ukrainian border.
Both sides have significantly escalated their long-range attacks this year, causing a spike in civilian deaths, according to the United Nations.
“At this moment, 13 people have been killed” in the attack on Nizhnekamsk, the regional press service said in a statement on Monday.
Another 75 people were wounded, 21 of which had been hospitalized, the authorities added.
Russia’s Tatarstan region is rich in energy resources and has many major oil refineries that Kyiv has been targeting in retaliatory strikes.
Unverified footage on social media showed a large black smoke cloud billowing at the site of an oil facility.
Ukraine’s General Staff said it had struck the Taneko refinery, controlled by oil giant Tatneft, as part of a campaign of “reducing the military potential of the Russian aggressor.”
Russia’s Investigative Committee, which probes major crimes, said a child was among those killed.
So too were citizens from Tajikistan and Uzbekistan, according to the regional government.
Russia also hit Ukraine with deadly strikes on Monday.
Near the front line, a Russian artillery strike killed five people in a village in the northeastern Kharkiv region, local Ukrainian officials said.
“On August 10, Russian forces carried out a massive artillery strike on the residential area of the village of Bugaivka in the Chuguiv district. Various houses were destroyed as a result of the enemy attack. Five people were killed,” regional prosecutor’s office said in a statement on Telegram.
It posted a picture of a house reduced to rubble by the attack.
Russia’s defense ministry said it shot down 456 Ukrainian drones fired overnight. It never states how many reached their targets.
The Tatarstan region had earlier reported a “massive” Ukrainian drone attack.
Ukraine’s air force said Russia fired 126 drones in its overnight attack.
A woman was also killed in a Ukrainian attack on the Russian border region of Belgorod, and a man was killed in a Russian drone strike on a taxi in the frontline Kherson region, officials there said.
In Ukraine’s southern Odesa region, tens of thousands of households were still without power after Russian struck the power grid over the weekend.
Concerns are rising in Kyiv over the upcoming winter, with the energy network still reeling from four years of Russian strikes.
Last winter, millions were plunged into darkness and had their heating and water cut for hours as temperatures sunk to -20°C.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned on the weekend that his country has “virtually no intact thermal power plants” following the Russian attacks.
Kyiv has also been running short of vital missile interceptors as Russia has significantly escalated its attacks with hard-to-intercept ballistic missiles.
Dozens have been killed in Kyiv over the last two months in direct hits on apartment buildings.

item.title: HSC admission based on GPA scores; around 25 lakh seats available
item.description:
Admission to Class XI at higher secondary level will be conducted online based on students' GPA scores in the SSC and equivalent examinations and their preferred choice of colleges, with no admission test or lottery.
There are around 25 lakh seats available for HSC admission across the country, while the admission process is expected to be completed by September 15, said Inter-Education Board Coordination Committee President and Dhaka Education Board Chairman Professor Syed Akhtaruzzaman.
He disclosed the information while answering questions from journalists at a press conference held at the Ministry of Education at the Secretariat on Monday following the publication of the results of the SSC and equivalent examinations.
"The admission process will be completed by September 15 and classes for the new academic year will begin immediately afterwards," he said.
The date for the start of classes will be announced soon through a notification, he added.
Regarding the number of available seats, Syed Akhtaruzzaman said there are around 25 lakh seats at the HSC level across the country.
"Last year, 58.7% of these seats were filled, while around 41.3% remained vacant," he said.
He expected the number of vacant seats to increase further this year in proportion to the number of eligible students.
Explaining the admission procedure, he said no student would be admitted through a lottery or admission test. Under the existing system, students will be allocated colleges and seats based on their GPA scores in the SSC and equivalent examinations and the order of preference stated in their applications.
He said the schedule and timeline for Class XI admission have already been set and a detailed notification and admission policy would be issued soon.

item.title: Bangladeshi philosopher Iqramlemagne receives industry recognition
item.description:
Iqramlemagne is a Bangladeshi philosopher who gained the title “Father of Hospitality” for his influential role in establishing hospitality as both the “industry of industries” and a recognized field of philosophical thought.
His most renowned philosophical expression is hospitalitas, industria industriarum (“Hospitality, the industry of industries”; French: “L'hospitalité, l'industrie des industries”).
Iqramlemagne introduced the term “hospitalitian,” an industry-specific designation for professionals working in hospitality.
A hospitalitian represents anyone committed to the practice of welcoming, hosting, and serving guests with care and professionalism.
He developed hospitality as a formal area of philosophy, moving the industry’s focus beyond technical vocational training toward broader themes of ethics, human relationships, institutional values, and social interaction.
The hospitality sector has a far-reaching economic influence, with industries worldwide adopting hospitality principles.
It is deeply connected with real estate, agriculture, technology, and many other fields, combining global standards with local traditions and expertise.
From the development of ancient roadside inns to today’s digital concierge platforms, hospitality’s ability to respond to social and technological changes remains a key driver of global growth and prosperity.
The Iqramlemagne Equation suggests that authentic hospitality is not a one-sided act of service or submission. Instead, it is a balanced relationship built on mutual respect between the host (Hospitalitian) and the visitor (Guest).
The “I Love Hospitality” campaign represents an initiative focused on improving professional standards, motivating future generations, and highlighting the rewarding career opportunities available within the hospitality industry.
He advocates a model that combines traditional indigenous guest-welcoming customs with contemporary hospitality science and sustainable practices.
Through awareness campaigns, Iqramlemagne has supported the acceptance of tipping culture in Bangladesh as a way to financially strengthen hospitality professionals and improve recognition of their contributions.
He is widely associated with the statement: “The greatest medicine for modern society is hospitality.”
Iqramlemagne serves as chief of hospitality at The Aristocrat Lounge and is a founding president of the Association for the Advancement of Hospitality (AAH).
Through these roles, he continues to connect traditional hosting values with modern hospitality management and operational excellence.

item.description:
Maintaining its streak of success, Nasima Kadir Molla High School and Homes in Narsingdi has once again achieved an outstanding result in the Secondary School Certificate (SSC) examinations. All 382 students who appeared for the examinations from the institution this year passed, with every one of them achieving GPA 5.

Immediately after the results were published at 10:00 am today, Monday, the examinees and current students of the institution celebrated by dancing and singing. Teachers and guardians also joined in the celebrations. Guardians brought packets of sweets, while students were seen embracing one another and celebrating their success.

SSC, equivalent results published: Pass rate 64.05pc, 106,009 obtain GPA-5

According to students and guardians, the excellent result was made possible by the teachers’ tireless efforts, proper guidance, regular classes, special classes, regular home visits by guide teachers, tutorials and monthly examinations.

Miloy Debnath, a science-group student who achieved GPA 5, said, “All my friends, including me, got GPA 5. So we are all dancing, singing and celebrating together. After achieving such a result, I have forgotten all the hardship of our efforts. My parents are happy, and what could be more joyful than that?”

According to the school’s administrative department, Nasima Kadir Molla High School and Homes has been achieving good results in the Primary Education Completion (PEC), Junior School Certificate (JSC), and SSC examinations since its establishment in 2008.

The institution continued that success this year as well. Of this year’s examinees, 376 were from the science group and six from the business studies group. All of them achieved GPA 5.

The institution’s head teacher told Prothom Alo, “After analysing the overall results across the country, it appears that we are among the best-performing institutions in the country. The school chairman’s innovative thinking and timely guidance are the main reasons behind this good result. We never allow our teachers and students to become disconnected from one another. Besides, our teachers and students work so hard that good results are bound to follow. We want to maintain our position among the country’s best not only in academic results but also in co-curricular activities.”

Last year, all 320 students who appeared for the examinations also achieved GPA 5. In addition, 293 of 294 students achieved GPA 5 in 2024; 270 of 278 in 2023; all 266 in 2022; 237 of 247 in 2021; 200 of 214 in 2020; 168 of 171 in 2019; 137 of 139 in 2018; and all 164 in 2017.

Nasima Kadir Molla High School and Homes was established in 2008 in the Velanagar area of Narsingdi town by Abdul Kadir Molla, chairman of Thermex Group, and his wife Nasima Begum, with a commitment to providing quality education in Narsingdi.

The school is currently run under strict discipline with the overall supervision of 174 young and talented teachers. It currently has 5,200 students.

School founding president and chairman of Thermex Group, Abdul Kadir Molla, said, “My wife Nasima Begum and I established the institution with a commitment to providing quality education in a town like Narsingdi.”

“We have always wanted students to become human resources through proper education. Our institution has consistently achieved good results. This year, too, it has maintained its streak of being among the country’s top performers by achieving a 100 per cent pass rate with 100 per cent GPA 5s. I congratulate the examinees, teachers and guardians,” he added.

item.title: itel launches air conditioner suitable for Bangladeshi households
item.description:
Global smart lifestyle brand itel has entered Bangladesh's consumer electronics market with the launch of its first air conditioner, marking the brand's expansion beyond smartphones and smart devices.

The itel ‘DC Inverter Air Conditioner’, manufactured in Bangladesh, is the first product under the brand''s new consumer electronics portfolio. Designed to deliver consistent cooling while reducing electricity consumption, the model is tailored to the needs of Bangladeshi households.

The air conditioner features DC Inverter Technology, which automatically adjusts the compressor speed according to cooling demand instead of repeatedly switching it on and off. According to itel, this helps reduce electricity consumption by up to 70 per cent, ensures stable cooling and extends the compressor's lifespan. The model also comes with a 12-year compressor warranty, a 5-year warranty on spare parts, and 5 years of free service support.

“This air conditioner has been developed by considering local climate conditions, power supply and consumer needs so that reliable, energy-efficient cooling becomes more accessible,” said Donssion, Overseas General Manager of itel. He added, "We are delighted to expand our consumer electronics business in Bangladesh, a market where we have built a strong presence over the years. Bangladesh is one of our most important strategic markets.”

The air conditioner also features Triple Voltage Care technology, designed to protect against low and high voltage as well as sudden fluctuations, and a four-way airflow system intended to distribute cool air more consistently across a room.

The product is now open for pre-booking through authorised itel brand outlets and national partner retail channels nationwide, with market availability expected by late August. itel has partnered with Carlcare to provide installation, maintenance and technical support through a network of more than 700 service centres across the country.

Operating in more than 70 emerging markets, itel is a leading brand under TRANSSION Holdings. The brand has built a strong customer base in Bangladesh through its smartphones, feature phones, accessories and smart devices, and plans to further expand its consumer electronics portfolio with more home appliances in the future.

item.title: We are on the ‘Yes’ side, now they have become the ‘No’: Jamaat ameer
item.description:
Opposition Leader and Jamaat-e-Islami Ameer Shafiqur Rahman has called on the BNP (Bangladesh Nationalist Party) to accept the people’s verdict, saying the country should be built on justice and equal rights for all.

“We want to stop the activities of extortionists and corrupt people. We want to build a Bangladesh where everyone has equal rights based on justice and fairness. That is what we want to ensure. That is why there was a referendum. Those who are now in government also asked people to vote ‘Yes’. Now we are on the side of ‘Yes’, while they have become ‘No’,” he said.

Shafiqur made the remarks as the chief guest at a public rally organised today, Monday, by Jamaat-e-Islami at the Bonarpara Government Kazi Azhar Ali Model High School ground in Saghata upazila of Gaibandha.

The rally was presided over by district unit Naib-e-Ameer and Gaibandha-5 MP Abdul Wares.

Calling on the BNP to accept the people’s verdict, the Jamaat chief said those who ignored the people’s verdict in the past had failed to remain in power, find peace or consolidate their authority.

“We are clearly saying that those who disregard the people’s verdict have never survived, found peace or been able to consolidate power. The elections of 2014, 2018 and 2024 are proof of that. Accept the people’s verdict. Close the path to fascism, carry out reforms and open the way for a humane and democratic state,” he said.

Shafiqur said his party would provide full cooperation to the government as an opposition party, but warned against what he described as a return to the path of authoritarianism.

“Those who walk this path will have to flee. This is the path of fleeing. If you follow this path, you will not be able to go to Mecca, you will go to Delhi. The final destination on this path is Delhi. The people of this country do not want Delhi’s interference or any form of domination,” he said.

Referring to the political violence of the past 15 years, Shafiqur said both the incumbent government and Jamaat had been victims of repression.

“Why would the oppressed become oppressors again?” he asked.

He alleged that five Jamaat members had been killed since the formation of this government.

“Do we want a rule of murder to be established again? No, we do not. Be careful. Stop here, full stop. Do not take another step towards killing,” he said.

The Jamaat ameer also warned that the country’s youth would not be intimidated.

“Even if you try a thousand times, you will not be able to become fascists. But you are taking steps in that direction,” he said.

Saying that no form of fascism would be tolerated in Bangladesh, Shafiqur said, “Fascism does not belong to any particular party. Fascism is a virus. The people no longer want fascism.”

He called on people to be prepared to take to the streets again if necessary.

“Perhaps we will have to take to the streets again. For the sake of the nation, we will do so not once but a hundred times, InshaAllah,” he said.

Jamaat Assistant Secretary General Abdul Halim, Gaibandha-1 MP Majedur Rahman, Gaibandha-2 MP Abdul Karim, Gaibandha-3 MP Nazrul Islam and Islami Chhatra Shibir Central Secretary General Sibgatullah Sibga, among others addressed the rally.

Earlier, at around 10:15 am, Shafiqur went to Bonarpara and visited the graves of Chhatra Shibir activists Saifullah Bari and Salahuddin, who were killed in an attack on 21 June. He also expressed condolences to their families and provided them financial assistance.

item.title: DU female students hold solidarity rally, demand abolition of curfew
item.description:
A group of female Dhaka University students under the banner of Oborodhbashini held a solidarity rally at the Raju Sculpture on Monday, demanding the abolition of the evening curfew in female residential halls.
The curfew currently restricts female students from entering or leaving their halls between 10pm and 6am.
The rally was organized by the Oborodhbashini platform, with solidarity expressed by the University Teachers’ Network, left-leaning student organizations and feminist groups.
Female students have been protesting for the past few days, demanding the withdrawal of the curfew from the university’s female residential halls.
The protesters have collected consent signatures from students and submitted memorandums to the vice-chancellor twice, outlining three demands. On Sunday, they issued a 48-hour ultimatum, warning that they would announce tougher programs if their demands were not addressed.
Their demands include the immediate abolition of the 10pm-6am curfew in female halls, along with ensuring 24-hour unrestricted movement and overall security for female students.
They also demanded that female students be allowed to enter any female hall by showing a valid ID card and stay overnight with proper permission, and that female relatives be allowed to enter the halls.
Speaking at the rally, Shirin Haque of Naripakkha, a women's rights platform, said the curfew had previously been imposed from 6pm to 6am.
“We protested at that time, and then the time was set to 10pm to 6am. We were able to extend the time, but the discrimination still continues,” she said.
Expressing solidarity on behalf of the University Teachers’ Network, Dhaka University Economics Department Associate Professor Rushad Faridi said the demand had been raised for many years.
“There is no doubt that this is a highly discriminatory rule. We have now moved from July into August. Following the July uprising of 2024, August marked the beginning of a new independence for us. Yet, even in this new Bangladesh, such a discriminatory and oppressive rule still remains. As teachers, this is deeply embarrassing for us,” he said.
He questioned why female students could return home late at night but were not allowed to return to campus after 10pm.
“If women can return to their homes at 11pm, midnight, or even 1am, why can’t they return to campus? What could be a greater example of discrimination than this? Does this mean that we, as university teachers, are incapable of ensuring the safety of our female students after 10pm? That seems to be the implication, doesn’t it?” he said.
Faridi called for the immediate repeal of the rule.
Under the existing rules, female DU students cannot enter or leave their halls between 10pm and 6am. If necessary, they must obtain prior permission from their house tutors through a late pass.
In emergencies, the authorities contact the students’ local guardians before allowing them to leave the halls.

item.title: PM mourns deaths of 16 Bangladeshis in Saudi fire
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has expressed grief over the deaths of 16 Bangladeshi nationals in a factory fire in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.
In a condolence message sent to the media on Monday, the prime minister expressed sympathy to the bereaved families and assured them of all necessary assistance.
Prime Minister’s Press Secretary Saleh Shibli said the prime minister was keeping a constant update on the matter.
He said the prime minister had instructed the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment, and the Bangladesh mission in Riyadh to take coordinated initiatives to bring the bodies of the deceased back to Bangladesh.
He also instructed the relevant ministries to take coordinated steps to repatriate the bodies as soon as possible. The Prime Minister’s Office will provide all necessary assistance for the process.
The 16 Bangladeshis died in a fire at a sofa manufacturing factory in Riyadh on Sunday.

item.title: 87,309 religious institutions to get honorarium in FY27
item.description:
A total of 87,309 religious institutions will come under the state honorarium program in the 2026-27 fiscal year, benefiting 2,56,074 religious leaders working at the institutions. Of the institutions, 82,656 are mosques, 3,000 temples, 752 Buddhist monasteries and 301 churches.
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is scheduled to inaugurate the program this month.
The decision was taken at a recent meeting of the cell formed to implement the government’s election manifesto to introduce a monthly honorarium and training-based welfare system for mosque imams, muezzins, khadems and other religious leaders of other faiths.
The meeting was chaired by PM’s Adviser on Public Administration and cell president Md Ismail Zabihullah.
In the 2026-27 fiscal year, 15 mosques will be selected from each union for the honorarium program.
In municipalities, four mosques will be selected from each ward of ‘A’ class municipalities, three from each ward of ‘B’ class municipalities and two from each ward of ‘C’ class municipalities. In addition, six mosques will be selected from each ward of a city corporation.
For temples, five will be selected from each upazila. Of these, two will be selected from each ward of ‘A’ class municipalities and one from each ward of other classes. The remaining temples will be selected at the union level.
The number of Buddhist monasteries and churches will be determined at a rate of 25% district-wise.
Under the program, each selected mosque imam, temple priest, Buddhist monastery principal and church priest will receive a monthly honorarium of Tk 5,000.
A mosque muezzin, temple serviceman, Buddhist monastery vice-principal and church assistant priest will receive Tk 3,000 each, while a mosque khadem will receive Tk 2,000 per month.
The honorarium will be transferred directly to the beneficiaries’ bank accounts through electronic fund transfer (EFT).
In the current fiscal year, Tk 1,100 crore has been allocated to provide monthly honorariums to religious leaders working at mosques and other places of worship.

item.title: Savar couple forced to cross neighbour’s roof to leave home
item.description:
An elderly couple in Savar has been forced to climb a 10-12-foot brick wall and cross a neighbour’s rooftop every time they need to leave their home after their access to the road was allegedly blocked by a wall built in front of their main gate.
The couple, who have lived in their home for more than three decades, say they have been facing the ordeal for nearly eight years.
The incident took place in the Nogorchar area of Rajfulbaria under Tetuljhora union in Savar.
Anisur Rahman, originally from Manpasha village in Jhalokathi Sadar, and his wife, Rashida Begum, bought four decimals of land in Rajfulbaria in 1995 and built their home there.
During a recent visit, this correspondent found the couple using a wooden ladder to climb onto a neighbour’s rooftop before making their way outside. At their age, the risky route has made even routine activities, such as going to a hospital or buying essential items, difficult.
Anisur alleged that Aslam, the brother of former union member Ayub, had tried to buy his land for Tk10 lakh during the previous Awami League government.
“I refused to sell the land. Later, Aslam allegedly built a wall in front of our gate, cutting off our access to the road. Since then, we have had to use a ladder and cross a neighbour’s roof to leave our home,” he said.
Anisur said the couple had been using the makeshift route for about eight years.
Rashida said the situation becomes particularly difficult when someone in the family falls ill.
“Taking a sick person to hospital is extremely difficult because we have to cross another person’s rooftop first,” she said.
Aslam was unavailable for comment when this correspondent visited the area.
However, Ziaur Rahman, manager of Aslam’s house, said Aslam had purchased four decimals of land from a person named Reza.
He claimed that Anisur later had a road recorded alongside his property in the BS record. A case has since been filed in court seeking cancellation of the record, he said.
Aman Ullah Aman, MP for Dhaka-2, said he was looking into the matter.
“If the affected family contacts me, I will try to resolve the issue as soon as possible,” he said.
Dhaka Deputy Commissioner Farida Khan said the field administration had been instructed to take necessary action.
“If the land has been illegally occupied, action will be taken against those responsible,” she said.

item.title: Bogra leads Rajshahi Board in SSC results
item.description:
Bogra has secured the top position in both the number of GPA-5 achievers and overall pass rate in this year’s SSC (Secondary School Certificate) and equivalent examinations under the Rajshahi Education Board.
A total of 5,900 students from Bogra educational institutions obtained GPA-5, while the district also recorded the highest pass rate, according to results published on Monday.
The overall pass rate in the Rajshahi Board stood at 77.63%, whereas Bogra achieved a district-level pass rate of 83.50%.
Notably, several renowned institutions in Bogra maintained their strong track record of academic excellence.
This year, a total of 180,310 students from eight districts under the Rajshahi Education Board appeared for the SSC examinations.
Of them, 139,983 students cleared the exams, resulting in a board-wide pass rate of 77.63%.
A total of 22,327 students achieved GPA-5, with the highest number coming from Bogra.
These figures were confirmed by Professor Md Ariful Islam, exam controller of the Rajshahi Education Board.
Among the top-performing institutions in Bogra, Bogra Zilla School led the way, with 217 out of 220 students securing GPA-5 and a 100% pass rate.
Bogra Government Girls' High School also achieved a 100% pass rate, with 237 out of 250 students earning GPA-5.
Biam Model School and College had 473 examinees, all of whom passed, and 399 obtained GPA-5. At Bogra Cantonment Public School and College, all 371 students passed, with 342 achieving GPA-5. The Armed Police Battalion Public School and College saw 347 students appear in the exam, all of whom passed, and 286 attained GPA-5.
RDA Laboratory School and College had 242 examinees, 149 of whom achieved GPA-5, with a pass rate of 99.59%.
At TMSS Public School, all 158 students passed, with 98 securing GPA-5.
Bogra Yakubia Girls' High School and College reported a 100% pass rate among its 244 students, with 169 earning GPA-5.
Mustafizur Rahman, principal of Biam Model School and College in Bogra, credited the consistent success of the institution to the collective efforts of students, teachers, staff, and guardians.
He expressed hope for even better results in the future.
Colonel Md Masud Rana, principal of Bogra Cantonment Public School and College, also acknowledged the vital role of the institution’s key stakeholders—including the chief patron, governing body chairman and members, teachers, and guardians—in achieving such outstanding results.
He also expressed optimism about maintaining this performance in the years to come.

item.title: Land acquisition delays keep two bridges unusable in Dumuria
item.description:
Two bridges in Dumuria upazila of Khulna were completed three years ago, but remain unusable as their approach roads have not been built due to unresolved land acquisition disputes.
The situation has left thousands of residents, including students, facing serious difficulties in travelling between villages on either side of the bridges.
According to the Dumuria upazila engineering office, construction of the 65-metre Kulati Bridge over the Mora-Bhadra River began in 2018 at a cost of Tk 4.64 crore to improve communication between Badurgacha and Kulati villages in Gutudia Union. The bridge was completed within three years.
However, disputes over ownership of land needed for the approach road emerged from the beginning. Despite the issue remaining unresolved for nearly eight years, the approach road has yet to be constructed, leaving the bridge largely unused.
Construction of the 84-metre Gajendrapur Bridge over the same river also began around the same time at a cost of Tk 4.84 crore to improve communication between Sahas and Sharafpur unions. The bridge was completed three years ago, but its approach road remains unfinished for the same reason.
Meanwhile, similar land acquisition complications have affected two other major bridges currently under construction in the upazila.
A 750-metre bridge over the Sharafpur-Gaoghara River is being built at a cost of Tk 119.52 crore, while a 461-metre bridge over the Kadamtala-Madartala River in Shovna Union is being constructed at a cost of Tk 67.55 crore. Land acquisition for their approach roads is also yet to be resolved.
Ram Prasad Mondal, one of the landowners whose property is needed for the Kulati Bridge approach road, said several investigations had been conducted into the issue, but 15-16 landowners on both sides of the bridge had yet to receive compensation.
Uttam Sarkar, a teacher at Kulati Secondary School, said residents had previously used a bamboo footbridge to cross the river. After it was removed following construction of the new bridge, local residents had to build bamboo stairs at their own expense to access the bridge.
“People have no choice but to take considerable risks to cross the bridge,” he said.
Mashiur Rahman Liton, a BNP leader, said the Gajendrapur Bridge was now being used to dry paddy instead of for transportation because it had no approach road.
He said communication between the two unions could be disrupted completely if the old bridge collapses.
Monoranjan Das, acting chairman of Sharafpur Union Parishad, said the failure to open the bridge three years after its completion was causing significant hardship for residents and hurting local businesses.
Dumuria Upazila Engineer Darul Huda said he had been trying to resolve the issue for the past two years, but the land acquisition process remained stuck in bureaucratic complications.
“We cannot construct the approach roads until the land acquisition issue is resolved,” he said.
Dumuria Upazila Nirbahi Officer Sabita Sarker said the administration was making efforts to resolve the issues involving the Kulati and Gajendrapur bridges.
Khulna-5 MP Ali Asgar Lobby said effective measures would be taken soon to make the two bridges operational.

item.title: 6 metal objects unearthed by shovel lead to discovery of 96 landmines
item.description:
Workers were digging soil to build a house. At that time they discovered six metal objects, found in the ground after hitting one of those with a shovel. Two days later, an army bomb-disposal team excavated the site and recovered 96 landmines.

The incident took place in Betbaria village of Gangni upazila in Meherpur.

The bomb-disposal team from Jashore Cantonment arrived at the site at around 1:30 pm today, Monday. Army personnel first examined the entire area with metal detectors before beginning excavation. Over nearly two hours, they recovered 96 mines, one after another.

Police and a team from the Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) cordoned off the area during the operation.

Gangni police station’s Inspector (Investigation) Shimul Kumar Das told Prothom Alo from the scene that the army bomb-disposal team arrived in Betbaria at noon and began excavating the site. Seventeen anti-tank mines and 79 anti-personnel mines were recovered. Most parts of the area were excavated.

After being recovered, the mines were taken to the nearby Madhugari field for disposal. The army was working to neutralise them there at the time of filing of this report.

Several police officials said an anti-personnel mine detonates when an object weighing 64 kgs is placed on it, while an anti-tank mine detonates under pressure from a heavier object.

The discovery of such a large stockpile of mines during excavation has caused considerable alarm in the area.

According to the army and police, the mines may have been buried by the Pakistan Army during the 1971 Liberation War for strategic purposes amid the wartime situation.

Mashiur Rahman, a local elder and former headteacher of a secondary school, said a Pakistani military camp had been located at Bengari field, about 10 kilometres from Betbaria village. Pakistani forces and freedom fighters fought a pitched battle there in 1971. The Pakistani forces were eventually forced to leave the area following a fierce attack by the freedom fighters.

The mines may have been left behind when the Pakistani forces withdrew, he said.

Several local elders and freedom fighters said Bengari field in Dharmadah village of Daulatpur upazila in Kushtia district lies about 2.5 kilometres from the site where the mines were discovered.

On 11–12 November 1971, freedom fighters fought a pitched battle with Pakistani forces at the field. Several freedom fighters and members of the allied forces, including Bir Protik recipient Waliul Hossain, were martyred in the bloody battle.

At one point, the Pakistani forces, overwhelmed by sustained attacks from the freedom fighters, fled towards Kushtia town through Betbaria village.

The mines may have been buried in an abandoned area of the village as they withdrew, the local elders and freedom fighters said.

Freedom fighter Golam Mostofa of Kajipur village in Kajipur union of Gangni upazila, who took part in the Bengari battle, told Prothom Alo by phone, “When we attacked the Pakistani force’s camp at Bengari in Daulatpur, the sun had not yet risen. Caught off guard by the sudden attack, the Pakistani forces fled towards Kushtia with their vehicles and tanks. We later captured the camp.

“The road where the mines were found in Betbaria was the route used by the Pakistani forces to flee with their weapons and equipment. They were attacked again in the Khalishakundi area on their way to Kushtia. Later, we blew up a bridge with explosives.”

Earlier, last Saturday, workers were digging soil on seven decimals of land owned by expatriate Bangladeshi Nuruzzaman Kalu in Betbaria village to construct a house. They noticed six metal objects while digging.

The objects were inscribed with the words: “PDFGL 63, Lot 37, Mine 1967.”

After being informed, police arrived at the site, cordoned off the area and strengthened security. Police contacted the army’s bomb-disposal team to arrange for the objects to be recovered.

Zaminur Rahman Khan, additional superintendent of police (Crime and Operations) in the district, told Prothom Alo that after the mine-like objects were discovered, the army bomb-disposal team was contacted. The site was also placed under police protection.

The army has recovered the mines and taken them into its custody. The process of neutralising them is under way, he added.

item.title: Bezos consortium nears deal to buy Liverpool stake: report
item.description:
SOCCER-FRIENDLY-LIV-ASM/

Amazon founder Jeff Bezos is part of a consortium nearing a deal to buy a one-third stake in Premier League club Liverpool, a report said Monday.

Sky News said Bezos was part of an investor group led by Amit Bhatia, the son-in-law of India steel billionaire Lakshmi Mittal, that also also includes Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin.

Liverpool owners Fenway Sports Group (FSG) confirmed the approach from Bhatia's group last month.

"An investment consortium led, managed, and represented by Amit Bhatia has expressed interest in making a strategic minority investment in Liverpool Football Club," an FSG spokesman told AFP.

Bhatia was until recently a shareholder in Championship club Queens Park Rangers.

The Sky report said the consortium was "closing in on a deal to buy a roughly one-third stake in Liverpool", with FSG preparing to make an announcement "as soon as this week".

Bezos, 62, is one of the world''s richest men, with a fortune estimated by Forbes magazine at more than US$280 billion, while Saverin's wealth is put at US$33 billion.

Bezos has reportedly explored previous bids for the NFL's Seattle Seahawks and Washington Commanders, but decided against pursuing either deal.

Sky said the investment in Liverpool, part of an influx of American money into the Premier League, would reportedly value the 20-time English league champions at US$6 billion.

FSG, which also owns the Boston Red Sox baseball team, bought Liverpool in 2010 for £300 million (US$405 million).

It sold a minority stake in the club in 2023 to US private equity group Dynasty Equity.

Liverpool won the Premier League title in 2024/25 under Arne Slot but the Dutchman was sacked in May after a turbulent season.

item.description:
Indian High Commissioner to Bangladesh Dinesh Trivedi left Dhaka for New Delhi on Monday after holding three meetings in Dhaka over the past 24 hours, which is seen as further consultations amid efforts to engage constructively to take forward relations between the two neighbours.

He met Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman on Sunday at State Guest House Padma, while he had separate courtesy meetings with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed at the Secretariat on Monday.

“Yes, he left Dhaka for New Delhi (on Monday),” a diplomatic source told news agency UNB, without elaborating, adding that the visit was “preplanned.”

During the courtesy meeting with the Bangladesh prime minister, Dinesh Trivedi conveyed greetings from Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi to Tarique Rahman and the intent to work together with the government and the people of Bangladesh in a “positive, constructive and forward-looking” manner.

They exchanged views on matters of mutual interest and discussed avenues for further strengthening bilateral relations between India and Bangladesh with a people-centric approach.

During his meeting with Home Minister Salahuddin, they discussed areas of common interest, including security cooperation between the two countries, and ways to further strengthen bilateral relations.

The high commissioner conveyed India’s willingness to strengthen people-centric cooperation in all domains, based on mutual interest, mutual benefit and mutual sensitivities.
